The studied cloak is a spherical transformation optics cloak discretized on a cubic lattice with spacing d = b/50.
The cloak has inner radius a and outer radius b, with b = 2a and wavelength λ = b used in simulations.
Emission rate inside the cloak can be inhibited by up to five orders of magnitude for radial dipole orientation near the center.
Emission rate shows strong spatial oscillations within the cloak shell due to local-field effects from the discrete lattice.
For a source outside the cloak, emission rate is close to free space except near the cloak surface where a modest enhancement occurs.
Doubling the size of discrete elements reduces the number of elements by a factor of eight and weakens the cloaking effect.
Discrete cloaks support leaky resonant modes that couple to the source and affect emission dynamics.
Material dispersion is modeled by Lorentzian profiles for permittivity and permeability, consistent with causality and Kramers-Kronig relations.
Material losses introduce nonradiative decay channels, reducing radiative emission enhancements.
The cloak behaves as a leaky multimode cavity with multiple electromagnetic modes inside the shell.
The Purcell effect explains the frequency-dependent enhancement or inhibition of emission inside the cloak.
Discrete geometry causes electromagnetic leakage between the cloak interior and exterior, unlike ideal continuous cloaks.
Local-field effects depend on the precise position of the source relative to the discrete lattice elements.
Emission rate depends strongly on dipole orientation, with radial orientation showing stronger inhibition than tangential.
The discrete dipole approximation (DDA) allows efficient modeling of the cloak's electromagnetic response including losses and dispersion.
The study uses both DDA and finite element methods to analyze spherical and cylindrical cloak geometries.
At certain resonant frequencies (~0.8b wavelength), the emission inside the cloak can be enhanced rather than inhibited.
The cloak's discrete structure leads to a non-flat spatial and spectral local density of states inside the cloaked region.
The emission rate formula involves the imaginary part of the field-susceptibility tensor at the source location.
The study highlights the importance of considering metamaterial discreteness in practical invisibility cloak designs.
